catalog_quote: Lewo is a “word stress language”, where each phonological word contains one peak of greater auditory prominence. The two primary rules of stress application in Lewo are firstly, that stress is counted backwards from the end of the word ... and secondly, that the final syllable is extrametrical. ... the stress peak occurs predictably on the penultimate syllable of the word. Secondary stres in polysyllabic words occur every second penultimate. ... There are a number of additional complications beyond this basic rule. First, it is noted that Lewo stress assignment is sensitive to syllable quantity or weight. In particular, syllables of the form (C)i are defined as “weak syllables”, ie. they are extrametrical, and do not count in allocating stress. ... monosyllabic lexemes ... carry stress equivalent to that found in the main stress of multi-syllabic words ... there are certain morpheme cla…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The record rests on the sole reference grammar of Lewo (Early 1994 ANU PhD, 556 pp), held both as the ANU text bitstream and the original PDF; the deciding quotation, locator (ch. 3, section 3.4, pp. 66-69) and the exception/monosyllable/prefix passages all verify verbatim in the text we hold. The classification (right edge, penult primary, alternating secondaries, (C)i 'weak syllables' skipped, hence weight-hedged) is a faithful reading of pp. 66-69. Glottolog and Crossref show no later phonology, prosody or instrumental work on Lewo, and Early himself says none existed; the only unheld descriptive item is his 4-pp 1995 dictionary introduction (low value). no reclassification or re-read indicated.
